_help: Track B: Hedging. Items are grouped by stage. See README.md, section 'How to add or edit an item'.
title: Hedging

items.prompt: Online learning may improve access to education for students in rural areas.
items.reason: “may” is a modal verb. It shows the writer is not completely sure.
items.hint: There is one. It is a modal verb.

items.prompt: The results suggest that regular exercise could reduce stress among office workers.
items.reason: “suggest” is a cautious reporting verb and “could” is a modal verb.
items.hint: There are two: a reporting verb and a modal verb.

items.prompt: Some students appear to learn more effectively in small groups.
items.reason: “Some” limits the claim to part of the group, and “appear” makes it less certain.
items.hint: There are two: a quantity word and a verb.

items.prompt: Higher taxes on sugary drinks are likely to reduce consumption in the long term.
items.reason: “likely” shows the result is probable, not certain.
items.hint: There is one. It is an adjective.

items.prompt: This trend is possibly linked to the rising cost of housing in major cities.
items.reason: “possibly” is an adverb that makes the link less certain.
items.hint: There is one. It ends in -ly.

items.prompt: Social media use might affect the sleep of some teenagers.
items.reason: “might” is a modal verb, and “some” limits the claim to part of the group.
items.hint: There are two: a modal verb and a quantity word.

items.prompt: Small businesses often find it difficult to obtain loans from banks.
items.reason: “often” means “many times but not always”, so the claim is less absolute.
items.hint: There is one. It is a frequency word.

items.prompt: The data indicate that the new policy has probably reduced waste.
items.reason: “indicate” is a cautious reporting verb and “probably” is an adverb.
items.hint: There are two: a reporting verb and an adverb.

items.prompt: Perhaps the main cause of the delay was a lack of communication.
items.reason: “Perhaps” is an adverb that shows the writer is not sure.
items.hint: There is one. Look at the start.

items.prompt: Most participants seemed to prefer the shorter version of the course.
items.reason: “Most” means “not all”, and “seemed” makes the claim less certain.
items.hint: There are two: a quantity word and a verb.

options: Noise reduces concentration.
Noise probably reduces concentration.
Noise may reduce concentration.
items.reason: No hedge is the strongest. “probably” means more likely than not. “may” means it is only possible.
items.hint: Which one has no hedge at all?
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: All students prefer online classes.
Most students prefer online classes.
Some students prefer online classes.
A few students prefer online classes.
acceptedAnswers: A few students prefer online classes.
items.reason: “All” covers everyone, “most” more than half, “some” an unknown part, and “a few” a small number.
items.hint: Think about how many students each sentence covers.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: Students always check their work.
Students usually check their work.
Students sometimes check their work.
Students rarely check their work.
items.reason: always → usually → sometimes → rarely: from every time to almost never.
items.hint: Think about how often each word means.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the most often and end with the least often.

options: It is certain that…
It is likely that…
It is possible that…
items.reason: “certain” means sure, “likely” means probable, and “possible” means it could happen.
items.hint: Which word means 100% sure?
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: The evidence proves that…
The evidence strongly suggests that…
The evidence may suggest that…
items.reason: “proves” is the strongest. “strongly suggests” is confident but careful. “may suggest” is weaker.
items.hint: Academic writers rarely use “proves”. Is it strong or weak?
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: The new rule will reduce traffic.
The new rule is likely to reduce traffic.
The new rule might reduce traffic.
acceptedAnswers: The new rule will reduce traffic.
The new rule is likely to reduce traffic.
The new rule might reduce traffic.
items.reason: “will” is a prediction with no doubt. “is likely to” is probable. “might” is only possible.
items.hint: Which one shows no doubt at all?
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: This is definitely the main reason.
This is almost certainly the main reason.
This is possibly the main reason.
acceptedAnswers: This is definitely the main reason.
This is almost certainly the main reason.
This is possibly the main reason.
items.reason: “definitely” shows no doubt, “almost certainly” a little doubt, and “possibly” a lot of doubt.
items.hint: “almost” makes a word a little weaker.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: There is clear evidence that…
There is some evidence that…
There is little evidence that…
items.reason: “clear evidence” is strong, “some evidence” is partial, and “little evidence” means almost none.
items.hint: “little evidence” means almost no evidence.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: Stress is the cause of the problem.
Stress is a likely cause of the problem.
Stress is one possible cause of the problem.
acceptedAnswers: Stress is the cause of the problem.
Stress is a likely cause of the problem.
Stress is one possible cause of the problem.
items.reason: “the cause” is the only cause; “a likely cause” is probable; “one possible cause” is one option among others.
items.hint: Compare “the”, “a likely” and “one possible”.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

options: The survey shows that students want more feedback.
The survey suggests that students want more feedback.
The survey might suggest that students want more feedback.
acceptedAnswers: The survey shows that students want more feedback.
The survey suggests that students want more feedback.
The survey might suggest that students want more feedback.
items.reason: “shows” is confident, “suggests” is cautious, and “might suggest” is the most cautious.
items.hint: Adding “might” makes a verb weaker.
items.question: Put these in order. Start with the strongest (most certain) and end with the weakest (least certain).

items.prompt: One small study of 20 university students.
options: Listening to music while studying improves memory.
Listening to music while studying may improve memory.
It could perhaps be possible that music might have some effect on memory.
acceptedAnswers: Listening to music while studying may improve memory.
items.reason: One small study is weak evidence, so one hedge (“may”) fits. The weak option uses so many hedges it says almost nothing.
items.hint: How much can one small study show?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: Many large studies in different countries agree.
options: Regular physical activity completely prevents heart disease.
Regular physical activity reduces the risk of heart disease.
Regular physical activity might possibly reduce the risk of heart disease.
acceptedAnswers: Regular physical activity reduces the risk of heart disease.
items.reason: When many large studies agree, a confident claim fits. “Completely prevents” goes beyond the evidence.
items.hint: Strong evidence allows a confident claim, but not an extreme one.
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: A survey of 40 students at one university.
options: All university students prefer online exams.
Some students at this university appear to prefer online exams.
It is perhaps possible that a few students might prefer online exams.
acceptedAnswers: Some students at this university appear to prefer online exams.
items.reason: A small survey at one university cannot speak for all students, so the claim is limited to “some students at this university”.
items.hint: Who did the survey actually ask?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: Several large studies agree, but a few studies found no effect.
options: Homework clearly improves results for every student.
Homework is likely to improve results for many students.
Homework could possibly perhaps have some small effect.
acceptedAnswers: Homework is likely to improve results for many students.
items.reason: Mostly strong evidence with some doubt fits “is likely to” and “many students”.
items.hint: The evidence is mostly positive, but not completely.
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: There are no studies yet. One teacher noticed this in one class.
options: Standing desks improve students' focus.
It is possible that standing desks help some students focus, but this has not yet been studied.
Standing desks might perhaps possibly have some kind of effect on something.
acceptedAnswers: It is possible that standing desks help some students focus, but this has not yet been studied.
items.reason: One teacher's observation is very weak evidence, so the claim must be cautious and say that it has not been studied.
items.hint: Is there any real research yet?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: A very large, long-term study, supported by many other studies.
options: Long working hours always cause serious illness.
Long working hours are linked to poorer health.
Long working hours might perhaps be linked to slightly poorer health in some cases.
acceptedAnswers: Long working hours are linked to poorer health.
items.reason: Strong evidence supports a confident claim (“are linked to”), but “always cause serious illness” goes too far.
items.hint: Strong evidence: be confident, but avoid “always”.
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: Two small studies found different results.
options: Video games improve problem-solving skills.
The effect of video games on problem-solving skills is not yet clear.
Video games may perhaps possibly affect something.
acceptedAnswers: The effect of video games on problem-solving skills is not yet clear.
items.reason: When studies disagree, the honest claim is that the effect is not yet clear.
items.hint: The studies do not agree. What can you safely say?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: A government report based on data from every school in the country.
options: Class sizes have increased in every school in the world.
Class sizes in the country's schools have increased.
It seems that class sizes might possibly have increased slightly in some schools.
acceptedAnswers: Class sizes in the country's schools have increased.
items.reason: Data from every school in the country is strong evidence, so a direct claim about that country fits. The world is not covered.
items.hint: How much of the evidence is missing?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: One online poll that anyone could answer.
options: Most people support the new tax.
The poll suggests some support for the new tax, but it may not represent the public.
Perhaps it might be possible that some people could possibly support the tax.
acceptedAnswers: The poll suggests some support for the new tax, but it may not represent the public.
items.reason: An open online poll is weak evidence, so the claim is careful and mentions its limits.
items.hint: Who answers an open online poll?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: A single case study of one company.
options: Four-day working weeks increase profits for all businesses.
A four-day week may have helped this company, but more research is needed.
Working weeks might perhaps possibly have some effect.
acceptedAnswers: A four-day week may have helped this company, but more research is needed.
items.reason: One company cannot speak for all businesses, so the claim is limited to that company.
items.hint: How many companies were studied?
items.question: Read the evidence. Which claim fits it best?

items.prompt: Social media causes depression in teenagers.
modelAnswers: Social media use may contribute to depression in some teenagers.
Heavy social media use appears to be linked to depression in teenagers.
items.reason: A link is not proof of cause, so “causes” becomes “may contribute to” or “appears to be linked to”.
items.hint: Change “causes” to a weaker verb phrase.
items.evidence: Several studies found a link, but they cannot show cause.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Online learning is worse than face-to-face learning.
modelAnswers: Online learning may be less effective than face-to-face learning for some students.
For some students, online learning appears to be less effective than face-to-face learning.
items.reason: Mixed results mean the claim should be limited (“for some students”) and softened (“may”).
items.hint: Add a modal verb and limit who it is true for.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Video games make children violent.
modelAnswers: Violent video games may increase aggressive behaviour in some children.
Playing violent video games might be linked to aggression in some children.
items.reason: A small, uncertain link needs a hedge (“may”, “might”) and a limit (“some children”).
items.hint: Use “may” and “some”.
items.evidence: Some studies found a small link; others found none.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Working from home increases productivity.
modelAnswers: Working from home can increase productivity for some employees.
Working from home appears to increase productivity in some jobs.
items.reason: Because results differ by job, the claim is limited to “some employees” or “some jobs”.
items.hint: Limit the claim to some workers or jobs.
items.evidence: Some surveys of office workers found this; results differ by job.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Fast food is the cause of obesity.
modelAnswers: Fast food is likely to be one cause of obesity.
Eating fast food regularly may contribute to obesity.
items.reason: Obesity has many causes, so fast food is “one cause”, not “the cause”.
items.hint: Change “the cause” to “one cause”.
items.evidence: Many studies link fast food to weight gain, but obesity has many causes.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Electric cars will solve the problem of air pollution.
modelAnswers: Electric cars could help to reduce air pollution.
Electric cars are likely to reduce air pollution in cities.
items.reason: There are other sources of pollution, so “will solve” becomes “could help to reduce”.
items.hint: Change “will solve” to something weaker.
items.evidence: Electric cars produce no exhaust fumes, but there are other sources of air pollution.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Students who use smartphones in class get lower marks.
modelAnswers: Students who use smartphones in class tend to get lower marks.
Smartphone use in class may lead to lower marks for some students.
items.reason: A pattern across several studies fits “tend to”: true in general, but not for every student.
items.hint: Use “tend to”.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Bilingual children are smarter than other children.
modelAnswers: Bilingual children may have some advantages in certain thinking skills.
Being bilingual appears to benefit some thinking skills in children.
items.reason: The evidence is about some thinking skills, not general intelligence, so the claim is narrower and hedged.
items.hint: Make the claim narrower: which skills?
items.evidence: A few studies found small advantages in some thinking skills.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Raising the minimum wage destroys jobs.
modelAnswers: Raising the minimum wage may lead to some job losses.
A higher minimum wage could reduce the number of jobs in some industries.
items.reason: When experts disagree, “destroys” becomes “may lead to some job losses”.
items.hint: Use a modal verb and a softer verb.
items.evidence: Economists disagree; studies show different results.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: Reading on screens damages children's eyes.
modelAnswers: Reading on screens for long periods may cause eye strain in some children.
Long periods of screen reading appear to be linked to eye strain in children.
items.reason: The evidence is about eye strain after long use, so the claim is narrower and hedged.
items.hint: Use “may” and say “for long periods”.
items.evidence: Some studies link long screen time to eye strain.
items.question: This claim is too strong for the evidence. How would you say it in an essay?

items.prompt: The results may possibly perhaps suggest that the new method could be somewhat effective.
options: The results suggest that the new method is effective.
The results prove that the new method is effective.
The results may possibly suggest the method could perhaps work.
acceptedAnswers: The results suggest that the new method is effective.
items.reason: One hedge (“suggest”) is enough. “prove” is too strong, and the last option still stacks hedges.
items.hint: Keep one reporting verb and one modal.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: It might be possible that online tutoring could perhaps help some students.
options: Online tutoring may help some students.
Online tutoring helps all students.
It is possible that online tutoring might perhaps help.
acceptedAnswers: Online tutoring may help some students.
items.reason: “may” and “some” are enough. “helps all students” is too strong.
items.hint: Which version uses only one hedge word plus “some”?
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: Evidence seems to possibly indicate that there may be a link between diet and mood.
options: Evidence suggests a link between diet and mood.
Diet controls mood.
Evidence seems to possibly suggest a link.
acceptedAnswers: Evidence suggests a link between diet and mood.
items.reason: “suggests” already shows caution, so no other hedge is needed. “Diet controls mood” is too strong.
items.hint: One cautious verb is enough.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: Exercise could perhaps possibly have some benefits for mental health.
options: Exercise has clear benefits for mental health.
Exercise might perhaps benefit mental health.
Exercise cures all mental illness.
acceptedAnswers: Exercise has clear benefits for mental health.
items.reason: With many large studies agreeing, a confident claim fits. “cures all mental illness” goes far beyond the evidence.
items.hint: Read the evidence. Is it strong or weak?
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: Perhaps it is likely that some customers may tend to prefer shopping online.
options: Some customers tend to prefer shopping online.
All customers prefer shopping online.
Perhaps some customers may tend to prefer it.
acceptedAnswers: Some customers tend to prefer shopping online.
items.reason: “some” and “tend to” are enough. Four hedges in one sentence make it weak and unclear.
items.hint: Keep “some” and one more hedge.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: Waiting times at hospitals might possibly have increased somewhat in recent years.
options: Waiting times at hospitals have increased in recent years.
Waiting times may perhaps have increased.
Waiting times have doubled everywhere.
acceptedAnswers: Waiting times at hospitals have increased in recent years.
items.reason: Data from all hospitals is strong evidence, so a direct claim fits. “doubled everywhere” adds facts the evidence does not give.
items.hint: Read the evidence. How complete is it?
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?
items.evidence: A national report using data from all hospitals.

items.prompt: Teachers might possibly perhaps consider giving feedback more often.
options: Teachers could consider giving feedback more often.
Teachers must give feedback every day.
Teachers might perhaps consider feedback.
acceptedAnswers: Teachers could consider giving feedback more often.
items.reason: One soft word (“could”) is enough for a polite suggestion. “must … every day” is too strong.
items.hint: Keep one modal verb.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. Which version is best?

items.prompt: This may possibly suggest that students could perhaps benefit from shorter lectures.
modelAnswers: This suggests that students benefit from shorter lectures.
Students may benefit from shorter lectures.
items.reason: Keep one reporting verb or one modal verb, not four hedges.
items.hint: Keep “suggests” or “may”. Remove the rest.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. How could you fix it?

items.prompt: It seems that it might be possible that remote work could reduce stress for some employees.
modelAnswers: Remote work may reduce stress for some employees.
Remote work seems to reduce stress for some employees.
items.reason: “may” (or “seems to”) plus “some” is enough.
items.hint: Start with “Remote work”.
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. How could you fix it?

items.prompt: It could perhaps be argued that sleep might possibly affect learning.
modelAnswers: Sleep affects learning.
There is strong evidence that sleep affects learning.
items.reason: Many large studies agree, so the claim can be confident. The hedges make it weaker than the evidence.
items.hint: Read the evidence. Does the claim need any hedge?
items.question: This sentence has too many hedges. How could you fix it?
